1.q: הַ⁠דָּבָ֞ר אֲשֶׁר הָיָ֤ה אֶֽל יִרְמְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה
1.note: See how you translated this clause in [7:1](ta:07).

1.q: שַׁלַּ֣ח אֹת֗⁠וֹ נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֛ן רַב טַבָּחִ֖ים מִן הָֽ⁠רָמָ֑ה בְּ⁠קַחְתּ֣⁠וֹ אֹת֗⁠וֹ
1.note: Jeremiah is describing one event, Nebuzaradan **sent him away**, before describing an event that preceded it, when Nebuzaradan **took him** from among the captives. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guards, took him and sent him away from Ramah]
See how you translated this name in 39:9.

The expression **he was bound in chains** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, Jeremiah implies that the Babylonian soldiers did it. Alternate translation: [and the Babylonian soldiers had bound him in chains]

The expression **the ones being exiled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, Jeremiah implies that the soldiers of the king of Babylon did it. Alternate translation: [whom the soldiers of the king of Babylon were taking into exile in Babylon]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 26:13.
The word **your** is singular here because Nebuzaradan is addressing Jeremiah. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **this place** represents Jerusalem and the people who lived there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against Jerusalem and its people]

3.note: The word **you** plural throughout this verse because Nebuzaradan is speaking about the people of Judah, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
See how you translated this expression in 9:13.

4.note: Nebuzaradan is using **in your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in your judgment” or “in your opinion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your opinion … your opinion … in your opinion]

The captain of the guards is using **I will set my eye on you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will take care of you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will look after you]

Here, **to your face** represents what is in front of Jeremiah and so is open and available for him to go to. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of the land is available to you]

4.q: אֶל ט֨וֹב וְ⁠אֶל הַ⁠יָּשָׁ֧ר בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֛י⁠ךָ לָ⁠לֶ֥כֶת שָׁ֖מָּ⁠ה לֵֽךְ
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about where Jeremiah thinks it is **good** and **right** to go after the command **go**. Alternate translation: [Go to the place that is good and right in your eyes to go]

4.q: אֶל־ט֨וֹב וְ⁠אֶל־הַ⁠יָּשָׁ֧ר בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֛י⁠ךָ לָ⁠לֶ֥כֶת שָׁ֖מָּ⁠ה לֵֽךְ
4.note: Jeremiah’s text has Nebuzaradan using the adjectives **the good** and **the right** as nouns to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [Unto whatever place seems best and most suitable in your eyes to go there, go]

5.note: See how you translated the names of these men in 39:14. This also occurs in verses 9 and 11.

6.note: See how you translated the names ** Gedaliah** and **Ahikam** in the previous verse. The word **Mizpah** is the name of a town.

The expression **the ones having been left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, Jeremiah implies that the Babylonians did it. Alternate translation: [the ones whom the Babylonians had left in the land]

7.note: Here, **the field** represents the open country outside of the cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 13. Alternate translation: [who were in the countryside away from the towns]
See how you translated the names ** Gedaliah** and **Ahikam** in the previous verse.

Jeremiah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and from the people of the land who were poor]

The expression **had not been exiled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, Jeremiah implies that the king of Babylon did it. Alternate translation: [from those whom the king of Babylon had not exiled to Babylon]

8.q: וְ⁠יִשְׁמָעֵ֣אל בֶּן נְתַנְיָ֡הוּ וְ⁠יוֹחָנָ֣ן וְ⁠יוֹנָתָ֣ן בְּנֵֽי קָ֠רֵחַ וּ⁠שְׂרָיָ֨ה בֶן תַּנְחֻ֜מֶת וּ⁠בְנֵ֣י עופי הַ⁠נְּטֹפָתִ֗י וִֽ⁠יזַנְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן הַ⁠מַּ֣עֲכָתִ֔י
8.note: The words **Ishmael**, **Nethaniah**, **Johanan**, **Jonathan**, **Kareah**, **Seraiah**, **Tanhumeth**, **Ephai** and **Jezaniah** are the names of men. The words **Netophathite** and **Maacathite** are the names of people groups, the people from the town of Netophah and the people from the region of Maacah. See how you translated “Gedaliah” and “Mizpah” in 40:6.

9.note: See how you translated these names in 40:5.

The word translated as **and** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [so that it will go well with you]

10.note: Gedaliah is using **behold me dwelling at Mizpah** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am going to stay here at Mizpah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will remain living at Mizpah]

Here, **to stand to the face of** represents being in front of someone to speak on someone’s behalf. Gedaliah is speaking of standing in front of the Chaldeans as a way of saying he will represent the people before them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to meet with the Chaldeans on your behalf]

Here, **wine** and **oil** represent the grapes and olives from which people make wine and oil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [gather grapes for wine and summer fruit and olives for oil]

11.note: Here Jeremiah is using the term **sons** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor, Ammon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and among the Ammonites] or [and among the descendants of Ammon]

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **remnant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the king of Babylon had allowed some people to stay behind in Judah]
See how you translated these names in 40:5.

12.note: The expression **they had been driven** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, Jeremiah implies that the Babylonians did it. Alternate translation: [from all of the places where the Babylonians had forced them to go]
See how you translated the similar phrase “gather wine” in 40:10.

13.note: Jeremiah is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the names **Johanan** and **Kareah** in 40:8 and the names **Gedaliah** and **Mizpah** in the previous verse.
See how you translated “who were in the field” in 40:7.

14.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 26:15.
The word **Baalis** is the name of a man.
See how you translated the similar expression in 27:3.

Johanan and the captains are using **to strike your life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to kill you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to murder you]
See how you translated this phrase in 40:11.

15.note: By **I will strike**, Jeremiah means that Johanan is asking to kill Ishmael. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will put to death]

Johanan is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and nobody will know]

15.q: לָ֧⁠מָּה יַכֶּ֣⁠כָּה נֶּ֗פֶשׁ וְ⁠נָפֹ֨צוּ֙ כָּל יְהוּדָ֔ה הַ⁠נִּקְבָּצִ֣ים אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אָבְדָ֖ה שְׁאֵרִ֥ית יְהוּדָֽה
15.note: Johanan is using the question form to urge Gedaliah not to let Ishmael kill him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not let him strike your life, so that all of Judah, the ones being gathered to you, will not be scattered, and the remnant of Judah will not perish!]

The expressions **the ones being gathered** and **be scattered** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use passive forms, you could express these ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. By **the ones being gathered** Johanan means that these people have come together to Gedaliah. When he uses the phrase **be scattered** Johanan does not say who would scatter them, so if necessary you could say that the people would scatter. Alternate translation: [and all of Judah, the ones who have come together to you, scatter]
See how you translated “strike your life” in the previous verse.

16.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **lie**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are saying what is not true]
